column1: # issue-taxonomy (harbor#512) — THE ONLY PLACE THE TYPE AND THEME SETS EXIST.
# Read by bin/issue-connector.sh and by nothing else that keeps its own copy. The
# reason this file exists rather than a list inside the connector: on 2026-09-16
# this estate measured SEVEN separate copies of one issue-type set in a sibling
# repo — two workflows, three scripts, a project board field and a branch-name
# regex — and widening it by two words meant touching nine sites across two
# alphabets. Two of the nine were found by a reviewer, not by the author.
# FORMAT: kind <TAB> label <TAB> glob|- <TAB> meaning
#   kind    `type` or `theme`
#   label   the GitHub label, verbatim. The connector never invents one.
#   glob    for a theme: a space-separated list of tracked-path patterns the
#           theme covers, used to SUGGEST a theme from what an issue names.
#           `-` for a type, and for a theme that is not path-shaped.
#   meaning one line. This is what a person reads when choosing.
# WHY GLOBS AND NOT KEYWORDS. A keyword->theme map is a hand-kept list and would
# drift the way the seven above did. A glob is checkable against the real tree:
# issue-connector-test.sh fails when a glob matches no tracked file, so a stale
# theme goes red instead of silently mis-routing. That check is the whole reason
# the third column is worth its cost.
# A THEME WITH `-` IS NOT SECOND-CLASS. `access` and `distribution` are about
# identities and registries that live outside this tree; a glob would be a
# fiction. The connector suggests nothing for them and says so, which is the
# honest answer rather than a guess.
# TYPES ARE NOT PATH-SHAPED AT ALL, by construction: whether something is a bug
# or tech-debt is a claim about the system's state, not about which files it
# touches. The connector reads a type from the issue body's `Type:` field, never
# from content.
# ── THE AXES (harbor#609, narrowed by harbor#612) ───────────────────────────
# This file declared `type` and `theme` and nothing else while the tracker ran 43
# labels; #609 widened it to seven axes. #612 then measured which of those seven
# anything actually READS, and the answer was sobering: across bin/, .github/,
# CONTRACTS/, docs/ and skills/ there is NOT ONE label filter. `fleet-L2` and
# `yard-L3` had THREE lifetime uses each. `P1-high` sat on 43% of open issues,
# which is a coin flip wearing a ranking's name. `phase:` restated the parent
# edge — three of its six values resolved to exactly one parent.
# So four axes remain, and each one is here because something queries it:
#   THE RULE IS STILL ONE LINE: A LABEL AN AGENT MAY APPLY APPEARS IN THIS FILE.
#   issue-connector.sh refuses anything else.
# CARDINALITY IS DECLARED BELOW AS DATA, NOT PROSE, and that is the #612 fix. The
# seven-axis table that stood here was a paragraph a human read and no checker
# did, so 32 issues violated `layer exactly one` and 13 violated `type exactly
# one` while every gate stayed green. A `#AXIS` row is parsed by --audit, so the
# rule and the mechanism cannot drift apart. Adding an axis means adding a row.
# FORMAT: #AXIS <TAB> kind <TAB> min <TAB> max <TAB> who sets it
#AXIS

column1: # `P0-critical` IS CAPPED AT THREE and the cap is the whole point of keeping the
# axis. P1/P2 were retired because 122 of 134 issues carried one and two values
# splitting 91% of a backlog rank nothing. A single rare flag can still mean
# something, and a flag that stops being rare has stopped meaning it — so --audit
# reports when more than three issues carry it, rather than trusting restraint.
# WHAT ORDERING REPLACED PRIORITY: the parent epic's body. #150 carries phase
# tables ordering 25 tickets and #591 carries ordered stages — ordering already
# lived there, and P1/P2 was the parallel copy that disagreed with nothing
# because nobody read it.
# RETIRED BY #612, AND WHAT CARRIES EACH FACT NOW:
#   layer      (140 applications) the repo, and the theme. Nothing queried it,
#              `helm-L0` was on 87% of open issues, and `cross-cutting` was used
#              as a MARKER on top of it, which is why 19 issues read as violating
#              a cardinality nobody had ever enforced.
#   P1 / P2    (122) ordering in the parent epic's body.
#   phase:     (21)  the native sub-issue parent edge.
# THE OWNERSHIP GRAPH IS NATIVE SUB-ISSUES (#612 Q2). `epic:*` stays a TYPE — it
# says what KIND of parent something is, which is not derivable — but membership
# is the edge, never the label. --audit reports an `epic:*` that parents nothing
# and a parent carrying no `epic:*`, because on 2026-09-21 there were five of the
# first and one of the second and nothing looked.
# THREE LABELS EXIST ON THE TRACKER AND ARE DELIBERATELY NOT DECLARED:
# `enhancement` (0 uses, duplicates `feature`), `high-priority` (0 uses,
# duplicates `P1-high`) and the bare `epic` (12 uses, superseded by the three
# `epic:*` types). Leaving them undeclared makes the connector refuse them, which
# is the behaviour wanted; deleting them from the tracker would rewrite 12 issues
# and is the operator's call, not this file's. Tracked in harbor#609.
